Breaking of Bread
BRAY-king uhv BRED
noun phrase
From Greek klasis tou artou (G2800 + G740); the breaking of bread practiced by the early church, embracing both common fellowship meals and the Lord's Supper (Acts 2:42, 46).

See also: Breaking of Bread

📖 Biblical Definition

The breaking of bread is the apostolic expression that describes the fellowship of the early church gathered around the table, embracing both their common meals and, preeminently, the Lord's Supper instituted by Christ. After Pentecost the new believers continued steadfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers (Acts 2:42). Daily they continued with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread from house to house, did eat their meat with gladness and singleness of heart (Acts 2:46). The Reformed faith confesses the Lord's Supper as one of the two ordinances Christ appointed for His church, in which the bread broken sets forth His body given and the cup His blood shed for the remission of sins. It is no bare memorial only, but a true communion of the body and blood of Christ, received by faith, in which believers feed upon Him spiritually and are knit together as one bread, one body (1 Cor 10:16-17). The breaking of bread therefore signifies both vertical communion with the crucified and risen Lord and horizontal communion among His people. The 1689 Confession teaches that worthy receivers, outwardly partaking of the visible elements, do also inwardly by faith receive and feed upon Christ crucified. Thus the early church's breaking of bread, marked by gladness and singleness of heart, is the abiding pattern of a people gathered in word, sacrament, and prayer.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The early church's table fellowship, embracing common meals and especially the Lord's Supper, a communion of the body of Christ.

BREAKING OF BREAD, noun phrase. From Greek klasis tou artou (G2800 + G740); the breaking of bread practiced by the early church.

Embraces both the common fellowship meals and, preeminently, the Lord's Supper instituted by Christ.

The believers continued steadfastly in it together with doctrine, fellowship, and prayers.

As it is written, 'And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers' (Acts 2:42).

A true communion of the body and blood of Christ, knitting His people into one bread, one body.

📖 Key Scripture

Act 2:42 — "And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers."

Act 2:46 — "And they, continuing daily with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread from house to house, did eat their meat with gladness and singleness of heart,"

1Co 10:16 — "The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?"

1Co 11:24 — "And when he had given thanks, he brake it, and said, Take, eat: this is my body, which is broken for you: this do in remembrance of me."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The breaking of bread is corrupted by reducing the Lord's Supper to a bare memorial or, oppositely, to a transubstantiated sacrifice, both departing from the Reformed confession.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The historic corruptions are doctrinal and remain. On one hand the supper has been made a propitiatory sacrifice in which the bread is supposed to become the literal flesh of Christ, robbing the once-for-all offering of Calvary of its sufficiency. On the other hand it has been reduced to a bare mental memorial, an empty sign emptied of all spiritual feeding.

The principle to recover is the Reformed and confessional middle, held by the 1689: the supper is no new sacrifice, yet no bare memorial either, but a true spiritual communion in which worthy receivers, by faith, feed upon Christ crucified. The bread broken proclaims His body given for sinners, and the fellowship of the table binds the church into one body until He come.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek klasis (G2800) and artos (G740) name the breaking of bread that marked the worship of the early church.

expand to see more

Greek klasis (G2800) — a breaking, used of the breaking of bread at the table

Greek artos (G740) — bread, a loaf; the element broken in fellowship and the supper

Greek koinōnia (G2842) — communion, fellowship, the sharing of the one bread

Greek klaō (G2806) — to break, the verb Christ used when He brake the bread

Acts 2:42 binds breaking of bread to doctrine, fellowship, and prayer in one ordered worship

Usage

"The breaking of bread united the early church in worship, word, and prayer."

"In the supper the bread broken proclaims Christ's body given for His people."

"The breaking of bread is communion both with the risen Lord and among His saints."
